newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU agrees new WTO finservices offer - Brittan.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees new WTO finservices offer - Brittan.

text.p: The European Union will offer to remove some restrictions on outside financial service firms to boost current talks on a global pact in the sector, Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said on Tuesday.

He told a news conference the new EU offer in World Trade Organisation (WTO) negotiations had been agreed by all 15 member states in Brussels earlier in the day and would be tabled in Geneva on July 1.

Brittan said the offer would confirm the present EU package which among other elements provides for free access to the Union's internal market for financial services on a most-favoured-nation (MFN) -- or non-discriminatory -- basis.

But he said it had been agreed among the top four trading powers -- the EU, the United States, Japan and Canada -- that they should set an example "by putting forward not only timely but better offers than previously...."
"Accordingly, we will be offering to eliminate 12 restrictions that still exist in the present schedule, and to limit the scope of a similar number of restrictions," he added.
These included elimination of the application of an economics needs test in the banking sector in Austria, and of the requirement in Belgium for incorporation in order to deal in securities.
The offer would also provide for an end to restrictions on investments abroad by Portuguese investment firms and on Portuguese residents offering their securities in foreign markets, Brittan said.
The WTO talks face a year-end deadline for agreement on a pact that would open up markets in developed and developing countries for banking, insurance and securities.
All offers are conditional on final agreement being reached by all the more than 40 countries in the negotiations.

Major powers had promised to make new offers by July 14 to give new impetus to the talks -- facing reluctance from key emerging economies to leave their infant financial service industries open to global competition.
A previous effort to shape a global pact broke down in 1995 when the United States said offers from major developing countries were not enough to justify it throwing wide its markets to all-comers.
An interim deal was put together under EU pressure by other countries in the talks, but that runs out on December 31 this year. Brittan said on Tuesday none of the participants wanted to renew it.
